  // enact the browser preference if "automatic",

  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">“Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Dinko Milaković
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Guido Cupani
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Bruce A. Bassett
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Stefano Cristiani
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Luca Pasquini
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> is the first application of spectral perfectionism to a high-resolution echelle spectrograph, reconstructing 1D spectra from 2D detector data via a forward model built on a calibration matrix of PSF shape, wavelength, and order trace, built entirely from laser frequency comb (LFC) observations. HARPS cannot resolve individual LFC lines, so each of 21 148 identified lines directly samples the PSF. We modelled these with a bivariate Gaussian, determining the PSF anywhere on the detector, calibrating wavelength, and tracing orders more accurately than the standard HARPS pipeline. Applied to 52.5 hours of HARPS data on quasar HE0515<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>4414, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> gives S/N comparable to, though slightly lower than, the standard pipeline. Its value lies in an exact resolution matrix and independent samples, properties standard extraction cannot guarantee for a non-separable PSF – a step toward better measurements of fundamental constants and exoplanet atmospheres.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_classification"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_classification">keywords</h6>spectrographs, spectral reduction, forward modelling, laser frequency comb, point-spread function
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_authorinfo"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">authorinfo: </span>Further author information: (Send correspondence to D.M)
<br class="ltx_break">D.M.: E-mail: dinko@milakovic.net, 
<br class="ltx_break">G.C.: E-mail: guido.cupani@inaf.it</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>INTRODUCTION</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The analysis of astronomical spectra starts with “spectral extraction”, i.e. the conversion of the information recorded on two-dimensional digital detectors into a wavelength calibrated and flux calibrated one-dimensional data, a representation of the true input spectrum. The “optimal” method for the extraction of spectra from digital detectors was developed in the 1980s with the introduction of charge-coupled devices (CCDs) to astronomical spectrographs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. The extraction process was since improved to compensate for curvature of spectral traces (particularly important for echelle spectrographs) and to improve the handling of the non-uniform response function of detector pixels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. A major simplifying assumption in optimal extraction is that the spectral traces are well aligned with the detector grid (columns and rows) and, consequently, that the point-spread function (PSF) of the spectrograph is a separable function of column <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and row <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. This assumption is rarely satisfied in practice and, unless specific steps are taken to correct for this, reconstructed spectra contain errors in flux estimates, wavelength calibration, and a degraded resolution. Such effects are particularly damaging for studies which rely on accurate measurements of line shapes and line centres, e.g. studies of fundamental physical constants, isotopic abundances, and atmospheres of exoplanets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we present the the first application of an advanced spectral extraction procedure, called “spectral perfectionism” (SP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, to observations made by an extremely stable, high-resolution echelle spectrograph, HARPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. Spectral perfectionism was shown to extract spectra to the statistical noise limit for an arbitrarily complicated PSF, without making assumptions about its independence in <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> components, and in the presence arbitrarily high and wavelength-varying foreground <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. However, this procedure requires a series of detailed information on the instrument (its calibration), as we briefly explain below. The resulting spectra are free from instrumental effects and are the closest possible representation of the incoming light – provided that the calibration is correct. Our motivation for this work was to assess whether spectral perfectionism offers tangible benefits for extremely precise measurements. We chose HARPS because it is equipped with a laser frequency comb (LFC), which we used to study the spatial variations of the PSF and to calibrate the spectrograph.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>SPECTRAL PERFECTIONISM FRAMEWORK</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Spectral perfectionism reconstructs the intrinsic object’s spectrum, represented by a vector <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math>, by combining the observed spectrum (vector <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}</annotation></semantics></math>) with the information contained in a “calibration matrix” <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>. This matrix is the collection of all available knowledge about the instrument, including the wavelength calibration, pixel response function, and the PSF shape as a function of detector position and wavelength <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Mathematically, the forward model is expressed as <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{f}+\mathbf{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐀𝐟</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{f}+\mathbf{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐧</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the pixel noise vector. Assuming normally distributed noise, the unbiased estimator for the input spectrum can be found via linear least-squares:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\hat{f}}=(\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{p}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐩</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\hat{f}}=(\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{p},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐍</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{N}</annotation></semantics></math> is the noise covariance matrix, defined as <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{ij}=\langle n_{i}n_{j}\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{ij}=\langle n_{i}n_{j}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>. Because the CCD pixels are assumed to have independent Poisson or Gaussian noise, <math id="S2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐍</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{N}</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly diagonal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The covariance matrix of this extracted spectrum is given by <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}=(\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A})^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}=(\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A})^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Because each resolution element illuminates several detector pixels, adjacent wavelength bins share illuminated pixels through PSF overlap, making the columns of <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> mutually non-orthogonal. As a result, <span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">C</span> has large off-diagonal elements and <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> suffers from extreme anti-correlated noise, known as covariance ringing. To suppress this noise, the spectrum must be reconvolved with a resolution matrix <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding a smoothed, physically meaningful spectrum <math id="S2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\tilde{f}}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{\hat{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\tilde{f}}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{\hat{f}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The central challenge is choosing <math id="S2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math> so that this reconvolution does not degrade the native instrumental resolution. In the SP framework, the analogous choice is <math id="S2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}\propto\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}\propto\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, which yields a reconvolved spectrum <math id="S2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{f}}\propto\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐩</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{f}}\propto\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, a global weighted sum of detector pixels with weights proportional to the PSF divided by the variance. Because <math id="S2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}\propto\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}\propto\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, the effective kernel applied to the spectrum is the noise-weighted auto-correlation of the line-spread function (LSF). For a Gaussian PSF of width <math id="S2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, this auto-correlation is a Gaussian of width <math id="S2.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\sqrt{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\sqrt{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, broadening the extracted LSF by a factor of <math id="S2.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and degrading the native resolving power by nearly 30%. To avoid this resolution penalty, Ref. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> proposed deriving <math id="S2.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math> from the symmetric matrix square root of <math id="S2.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> instead. We compute an intermediate matrix <math id="S2.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐐</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> defined by:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{2},\quad\mathbf{Q}=(\textbf{C}^{-1})^{\frac{1}{2}},\quad\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Q}^{T}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐐</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">C</mtext><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{2},\quad\mathbf{Q}=(\textbf{C}^{-1})^{\frac{1}{2}},\quad\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Q}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The final resolution matrix <span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">R</span> is constructed by row-normalising <math id="S2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐐</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> to ensure strict flux conservation. Writing <math id="S2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}=\sum_{j}Q_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}=\sum_{j}Q_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> for the row sums used in this normalisation, the reconvolved spectrum has an exactly diagonal covariance matrix, with uncertainty <math id="S2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}=1/s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}=1/s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> on each element <math id="S2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{f}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{f}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. The rows of <math id="S2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the unbroadened LSF at each wavelength bin, preserving the native resolving power of the spectrograph to within the accuracy of the PSF model encoded in <math id="S2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The calibration matrix contains all available knowledge of the instrument: the positions of illuminated pixels (the order trace), their central wavelength (wavelength calibration), pixel responses (flat-fields), as well as the PSF shape at each pixel. The most novel part of this work relates to using observations of HARPS’s LFC to construct the calibration matrix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The HARPS LFC is described in a series of articles, e.g. Refs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. Briefly, it produces <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 10\,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>10 000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 10\,000</annotation></semantics></math> modes with frequencies given by the formula <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{n}=f_{0}+nf_{rep}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{n}=f_{0}+nf_{rep}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the mode ordinal number (an integer), <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{rep}=$18\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>18</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">GHz</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{rep}=$18\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{0}=$4.58\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>4.58</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">GHz</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{0}=$4.58\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$</annotation></semantics></math> is the offset frequency of the first mode. The intrinsic width of one LFC line is <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{f}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">kHz</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{f}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$</annotation></semantics></math><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, whereas the full-width at half maximum (FWHM) of the HARPS resolution element ranges from <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">GHz</mi></mrow><mtext> to </mtext><mrow><mn>5.5</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">GHz</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}</annotation></semantics></math>, meaning that LFC lines are unresolved by HARPS. Consequently, the observed shape of a single LFC line is an excellent representation of the pixel-integrated PSF at that one detector position and wavelength. The idea was to map out how the LFC line shape vary across the detector, and use their known frequencies and positions to wavelength calibrate the spectrograph and trace echelle order centres.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/red_01_lines_on_detector.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Locations of identified LFC lines with raw detector counts in the background (red detector). Blue dots and red squares indicate the centres of LFC lines identified in fibres A and B, respectively, used subsequently for wavelength calibration and order tracing. The inset shows a 128 pixel wide and 32 pixel high rectangle containing 10 LFC lines per fibre.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We used a calibration exposure with LFC light feeding both HARPS fibres (referred to as fibres A and B), taken as a part of an ESO observing programme 0102.A-0697(A) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. The HARPS detector is a mosaic of two CCDs, covering diffraction orders 89 through 114 (red detector) and 116 through 161 (blue detector), which we treated separately. Each CCD consist of <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096\times$2148\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>2148</mn><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096\times$2148\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$</annotation></semantics></math> (in <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> directions, respectively), with the first and final 50 pixels in the <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> direction being pre-scan and over-scan regions (and were hence removed from further consideration, leaving a <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096\times$2048\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>2048</mn><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096\times$2048\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$</annotation></semantics></math> frame to work with). Running a maximum detection algorithm<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          We used <span id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">peak_local_max</span> from <span id="footnote1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">scikit-image</span> package <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>, we identified 5086 LFC lines falling on the blue detector (2729 appearing on fibre A trace and 2357 on fibre B trace) and 16062 falling on the red detector (8031 per fibre). Organising the lines into orders based on their proximity along the main dispersion direction, we retrieved full spectral ranges for orders 89 through 123, covering the wavelength range <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="$499.55\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$\leq\lambda\leq$691.45\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>499.55</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">nm</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>691.45</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">nm</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">$499.55\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$\leq\lambda\leq$691.45\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$</annotation></semantics></math>. LFC lines identified on the red detector are shown on Fig. <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We approximated the HARPS PSF shape with a bivariate (2-dimensional or 2D) Gaussian function. All 21148 LFC lines were independently fitted using this bivariate Gaussian function, with seven free parameters describing one line: amplitude <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, centre (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{x},\mu_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{x},\mu_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>), standard deviation (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>), rotation angle with respect to the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> axis (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, also used to measure the correlation between the elongation of the PSF in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> directions), and a zero-offset. We optimised model parameters using the Trust Region Reflective algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite><span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            As implemented in the <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">least_squares</span> function of a python package <span id="footnote2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">scipy<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="footnote2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">[</span><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a><span id="footnote2.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">]</span></cite></span></span></span></span>. The region considered was an <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11\times$11\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>11</mn><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11\times$11\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$</annotation></semantics></math> box centred on the brightest pixel. During parameter optimisation, we compared raw detector counts to the integrated flux under the Gaussian profile over the corresponding pixel area. For comparison, simply evaluating the Gaussian function at pixel centres resulted in 20% larger average values for <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>. We recorded the best-fit parameter values and their uncertainties in a FITS table for later use.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Left panel of Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the raw data and the best-fit Gaussian model for a randomly selected LFC line, with the right panel showing the corresponding normalised residuals: <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathrm{data}-\mathrm{model})/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var(data)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>data</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>model</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>data</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathrm{data}-\mathrm{model})/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var(data)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where model is our bivariate Gaussian at best-fit solution and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Var(data)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>data</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Var(data)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the variance on the data (all values are in electron counts). Some pixels have normalised residuals as large as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, bringing the reduced <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> statistic of the fit to <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi^{2}/\nu=9059" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9059</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^{2}/\nu=9059</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu=114" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>114</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu=114</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of degrees of freedom). Such high values are typical for all of our lines, but are not surprising, for the following three reasons. Firstly, variance on low-flux pixels is significantly smaller than the variance of high-flux pixels, resulting in unrealistically large residuals for the former. Secondly, besides including a zero-offset parameter, we did not model the spatially varying background light produced by non-linear processes in the photonic crystal fibre of the LFC system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. This background follows the order trace and, in the residual plot, can be seen going horizontally through the centre of the plot. Thirdly, spatial correlations in the residuals demonstrate that a bivariate Gaussian is insufficient to capture the full PSF shape and its asymmetry. The asymmetry of HARPS’s PSF is well documented from previous analyses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We pause here to comment on the retrieved 2D Gaussian parameter values. Figures <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> show the values of <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> obtained from all LFC lines, with clear evidence of continuous spatial variation. This is not trivially expected because each of the plotted <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim$10\,000$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>10 000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim$10\,000$</annotation></semantics></math> values (i.e. each dot in these figures is a single LFC line) were obtained independently, and there was no reason for best-fit parameter values to be correlated. These correlations are clearly seen in both the blue and the red detector, and there is a smooth change between the two detectors, consistent with them being caused by optical effects. Variations in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> are consistent with anamorphism, i.e. the angle that the detector makes with the grating is larger in the blue end of each order than in the red, such that the resolving power varies within the order. The blue detector shows a curious, but incomplete, pattern due to the blue cut-off of the LFC wavelength range. Variations in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> could hint to vertical astigmatism. Fibre B produced consistent results so is not shown. Observing such correlations from LFC line fits is a strong demonstration of the power that LFCs have in understanding how optical effects impact on instrument performance and for instrument diagnostics. It also supports the notion that we are indeed measuring PSF shape variations across the detectors.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/stamp_10013.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/176;" width="381" height="176" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Randomly selected LFC line on the red detector. Left: raw electron counts together with the centre (red cross) and <math id="S3.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> contours (red lines) of the best-fitting 2-dimensional Gaussian model. Right: residuals normalised by the statistical uncertainty on the data (including read-out noise). The large <math id="S3.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi^{2}_{\nu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>χ</mi><mi>ν</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^{2}_{\nu}</annotation></semantics></math> value (printed in the top right) is not surprising for reasons explained in the text. In the right panel, red indicates pixels where <math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{data}&gt;\mathrm{model}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>data</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>model</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{data}&gt;\mathrm{model}</annotation></semantics></math> and blue indicates the opposite. </figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/sigma_x_fibre_A.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/365;" width="381" height="365" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Standard deviation of the best fit 2-dimensional Gaussian function to individual LFC lines, projected along the detector’s <math id="S3.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> axis (<math id="S3.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math>), for fibre A. Each dot is a single LFC line we identified on both detectors, with colours indicating their <math id="S3.F3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> as per the colour bar to the right. The value of <math id="S3.F3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is a proxy for spectral resolving power, and varies smoothly across the detector plane in a correlated manner, consistently across both detectors, indicating connection with instrument optics. In the panels, wavelength increases to the right and to the top. </figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/sigma_y_fibre_A.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/364;" width="381" height="364" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Similar as Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, but for the projection of the PSF elongation along the <math id="S3.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-axis (<math id="S3.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>), tracing the size of the image projected by the optical fibre in the cross-dispersion direction. Also in this case, impacts of optical effects are clearly seen. </figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/rho_fibre_A.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/359;" width="381" height="359" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Correlation coefficient <math id="S3.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> (Eq. (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)) between the <math id="S3.F5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.F5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> components of the bivariate Gaussian PSF model, fitted independently to each LFC line on fibre A, plotted as a function of detector position. <math id="S3.F5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to a PSF that is exactly separable in the detector <math id="S3.F5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> frame and <math id="S3.F5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies the degree of non-separability. Correlation coefficients vary smoothly across the cross the LFC wavelength range but remain modest (<math id="S3.F5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|&lt;0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|&lt;0.1</annotation></semantics></math> everywhere).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the correlation coefficient <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> between the <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> components of the bivariate Gaussian PSF, computed from the fitted <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> for each LFC line on fibre A. The coefficient <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is calculated using the following equations:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
