<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{x}^{2}-\sigma_{y}^{2}\right)\sin(2\theta)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma_{x}^{2}-\sigma_{y}^{2}\right)\sin(2\theta),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(x)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sigma_{x}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta+\sigma_{y}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sigma_{x}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta+\sigma_{y}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Var</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(y)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sigma_{x}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta+\sigma_{y}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sigma_{x}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta+\sigma_{y}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The PSF is measurably non-separable across the full detector, but only weakly so, with <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> remaining below <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 0.08" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>0.08</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 0.08</annotation></semantics></math> everywhere. On the red detector, <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> varies smoothly and continuously, changing sign from positive at the bottom of the detector to negative toward the top. On the blue detector, <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is uniformly negative across nearly the entire fibre A trace. This pattern is consistent with the optical effects already inferred from the <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> maps (Figs. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), now expressed
directly in terms of the quantity that determines the validity of separable extraction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The next step was to wavelength calibrate HARPS using the known LFC line frequencies. To ensure unambiguous identification of LFC line modes, we created a look-up table containing the <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-coordinate and the wavelength of the central pixel in <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> direction (pixel number = 2048) for all 72 echelle orders. The mode identification algorithm first selected all lines within one order, isolated the line whose <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> was nearest to 2048, and then used the corresponding <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> value to identify the diffraction order number from the look-up table. The mode of this line was calculated as the integer nearest to <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=\lfloor(c/\lambda_{\mathrm{cen}}-f_{0})/f_{rep}\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>cen</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=\lfloor(c/\lambda_{\mathrm{cen}}-f_{0})/f_{rep}\rceil</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is the speed of light and <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{cen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>cen</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{cen}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the wavelength of the central pixel from the look-up table. Following the identification of the central line, we assigned modes to all other lines stepping by one mode.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We wavelength calibrated each order independently using the flexible Gaussian Process with a Matern <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu=3/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu=3/2</annotation></semantics></math> kernel, appropriate for performing regression on once-differentiable physical functions. Hyperparameters of the kernel (signal amplitude and length scale) were optimised by maximising the log-marginal likelihood on the pairs of values (<math id="S3.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{x},\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{x},\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. LFC line centre along <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and its wavelength. Derived Gaussian Process hyperparameter values are used later to obtain the wavelength of any given pixel. We confirmed the accurate identification of orders by comparing our wavelength calibration to an independent calibration produced by HARPS data reduction software (DRS) pipeline on ThAr arc lamp exposure taken on the same night, finding that the two match up to <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>250</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. For comparison, a single HARPS pixel spans a wavelength range corresponding to <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx$820\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>820</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx$820\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. more than three times larger than the discrepancies between our LFC calibration and DRS’s ThAr calibration. So far, we did not compensate for the uneven pixel sizes every <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}</annotation></semantics></math> in the <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, but we confirm that their effects are clearly seen in the wavelength calibration residuals (Fig. <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Compared to a normal distribution, the residuals are more centrally distributed, with zero mean and an root-mean-square of <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.06\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.06</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.06\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S3.SS1.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.41\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8.41</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.41\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>) for fibre A (B) on the red detector.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.06809v1/red_04_residuals_on_detector.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/235;" width="381" height="235"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Residuals to the wavelength calibration as a function of position on the detector. Effects from uneven pixel sizes are clearly seen in the form of sharp <math id="S3.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm$25\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>25</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm$25\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$</annotation></semantics></math> jumps every <math id="S3.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}</annotation></semantics></math> in the <math id="S3.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-direction.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we used the same machinery to accurately trace out echelle order centres by performing Gaussian Process regression on pairs of (<math id="S3.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{x},\mu_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{x},\mu_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>) values. Interestingly, the centres derived by us using LFC lines seems to better trace the geometric centre of the order than the traces stored in data products of the HARPS DRS (see Fig. <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). The same behaviour is seen for all 34 orders with LFC coverage, on both detectors. The DRS determines order traces by fitting a 1-dimensional Gaussian to the cross-section of the trace (i.e. in the cross dispersion direction) at a fixed number of points along the order and fits a low order polynomial through them. We visually inspected other files, taken on the same night, to better understand the reasons for the discrepancy and identify which set of order traces – ours or that of the DRS – should be used. We found that traces derived from LFC line centres (<math id="S3.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{x},\mu_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{x},\mu_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>) almost always traced the geometric centre of the order better than the DRS trace. The only exception was in the two bluest orders illuminated by LFC light, where we did not have full coverage. The cause for the offset of the DRS traces is unknown, and the impact on scientific analysis is unquantified.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/order_trace.png" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/141;" width="476" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Section of the LFC spectrum showing differences between the order trace obtained by fitting a Gaussian Process to centres of LFC lines and the traces stored in HARPS DRS data products, derived from a tungsten lamp observation taken on the same night (<span id="S3.F7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">HARPS_ORDER_TABLE_A.fits</span>). </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>HARPERFECT</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Computational Feasibility and Sub-image Extraction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Constructing a global calibration matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> for the entire detector simultaneously would require working with a sub-image of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096\times 4096\approx 17\,\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096\times 4096\approx 17\,\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> pixels, and a correspondingly sparse matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> of dimensions <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 17\,\mathrm{M}\times 4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 17\,\mathrm{M}\times 4096</annotation></semantics></math>, which is computationally prohibitive. Following previous implementations of the spectro-perfectionist approach (e.g., Ref. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>), we scale down the computational scope by processing localized segments of the detector rather than the entire frame simultaneously. Our implementation (<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span>) concentrates on extracting a single fibre of one echelle order at a time, reducing the size of the matrix to be inverted. We defined a geometric bounding box, i.e. a narrow extraction ribbon of approximately <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}</annotation></semantics></math> in height, containing the physical trace, and create a calibration matrix for that region of the detector. The height of the bounding box is determined empirically by extending the measured height of one order and padding it by <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}</annotation></semantics></math> either side. This reduces the sub-image to a manageable <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096\times 60" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096\times 60</annotation></semantics></math> pixels, and correspondingly <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="245{,}760\times 4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>245,760</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">245{,}760\times 4096</annotation></semantics></math>, allowing for a more rapid Cholesky decomposition, such that the extraction of the box takes approximately 50 seconds on a Macbook Pro from 2021.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Simulating the PSF for an Arbitrary Position</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The SP approach demands an estimate of the wavelength and of the PSF shape for every extracted pixel. This becomes easy with the machinery we set up in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> contains methods to return the wavelength at an arbitrary position within the echelle order from the Gaussian Process regression described Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Constructing the PSF shape for a specific pixel requires six parameters: the amplitude <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, the centre <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\hat{\mu}_{x},\hat{\mu}_{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\hat{\mu}_{x},\hat{\mu}_{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, the standard deviations <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\hat{\sigma}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\hat{\sigma}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, and the rotation angle <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mu}_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mu}_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is the centre of each of the 4096 physical pixels, and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mu_{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mu_{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> is calculated from the previously determined order trace from <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mu}_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mu}_{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. The values of the remaining four parameters (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{A},\hat{\sigma}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{y},\hat{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{A},\hat{\sigma}_{x},\hat{\sigma}_{y},\hat{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>) were obtained by interpolating between values saved in the FITS table containing the best-fit values of 2D Gaussian parameters fitted to LFC lines, together with their associated uncertainties, derived from procedures in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Also in this case, the interpolation was done using Gaussian Process regression to values (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>), where <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is each of the four parameters. An example of the regression for order 110 is given in Fig. <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.2 Simulating the PSF for an Arbitrary Position ‣ 4 HARPERFECT ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In order to produce a PSF image for an arbitrary location along the recorded spectrum, the user is asked to specify the location of the FITS table containing fits to LFC lines, the ordinal number of the echelle order of interest (an integer between 0 and 71, for compatibility with DRS products), the target fibre (A or B) and the pixel number along the dispersion axis (<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, a real number between 0 and 4095). The code automatically loads in the required information, performs Gaussian Process regression, saves intermediate products, and returns a wavelength and the PSF image. An example of the PSFs constructed in this manner are shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.2 Simulating the PSF for an Arbitrary Position ‣ 4 HARPERFECT ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> for 16 equidistant positions along the echelle order (every 256 pixels).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.06809v1/psf_cube_order50_fibreA_evolution.svg" id="S4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/126;" width="476" height="126"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Evolution of the PSF shape parameters within diffraction order 110, fibre A. To create a mock PSF, we evaluate the regression function (orange line with uncertainty bands) at the desired <math id="S4.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> coordinate and create a Gaussian PSF with the corresponding parameter values. Blue dots indicate the positions at which we created mock PSFs shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.2 Simulating the PSF for an Arbitrary Position ‣ 4 HARPERFECT ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.06809v1/psf_cube_order50_fibreA_gallery.png" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/365;" width="381" height="365" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Gallery of simulated PSFs at 16 locations within diffraction order 110. Each panel shows the reconstructed PSF at a different position within the order (every 256 pixels). In the first panel, arrows indicate the direction of increasing <math id="S4.F9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>. Text boxes report the values of <math id="S4.F9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\sigma}_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\sigma}_{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.F9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\sigma}_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\sigma}_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the rotation angle <math id="S4.F9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> of the PSF. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Workflow</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implemented the Spectro-Perfectionism mathematics as a custom Python pipeline. In its current state, the pipeline processes one spectral trace at the time. Parameters provided by the user at input are:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">path to the directory containing scientific frames to reduce;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">path to the FITS file with the output of the LFC analysis produced beforehand (see Sec.  <a href="#S3" title="3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), used to construct <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">A</span>;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">the order and fibre (A or B) to extract. For compatibility with DRS products, the order indices run from 0 to 71;</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The pipeline then processes all the science images within the directory through the following steps:</p>
<ol id="S4.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Ingestion:</span> For a given order/fibre combination, the pipeline loads the unextracted 2D science frame and queries the empirical LFC model to derive physical trace and crops a highly localized ribbon around it. At this time, we chose to use a pre-processed science frame, one of DRS intermediate products, i.e. a bias-subtracted, flat-fielded science exposures (using DRS nomenclature, <span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> ingests <span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CCD_corrected_science.fits</span> files). The main reason was to isolate the effects of wavelength calibration, order tracing and PSF reconstruction on the final products while developing understanding, trusting that the bias subtraction and flat-fielding is correctly performed by the DRS. Coincidentally, this also reduces the size of the calibration matrix <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, speeding up calculations. Future versions of the code will improve on this aspect.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Calibration matrix construction:</span> The pipeline defines its 1D extraction grid natively along the dispersion axis, corresponding one-to-one with the 4096 discrete physical columns of the detector. For each detector column <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, the central wavelength and the physical <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> centroid are evaluated directly from the empirical models derived from LFC lines. Concurrently, a 2D Gaussian PSF is generated (our model is already integrated over the pixel boundaries, Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), populating the corresponding column of the sparse calibration matrix <math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear inversion and deconvolution:</span> The sparse matrix <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math> and the diagonal noise matrix <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{N}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{N}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> are combined to compute the inverse covariance matrix <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐍</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐀</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{N}^{-1}\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>. The raw, high-variance deconvolved flux vector <math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\hat{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\hat{f}}</annotation></semantics></math> is then solved via fast sparse Cholesky decomposition.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Obtaining the final spectrum:</span> The pipeline computes the symmetric matrix square root of the dense inverse covariance (<math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}=(\mathbf{C}^{-1})^{1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}=(\mathbf{C}^{-1})^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>) and row-normalizes it to produce the flux-conserving resolution matrix <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math>. The raw deconvolved flux, <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\hat{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\hat{f}}</annotation></semantics></math> from step 3, is smoothed by the resolution matrix to suppress covariance ringing, and to produce the final spectrum: <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\tilde{f}}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{\hat{f}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\tilde{f}}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{\hat{f}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with a corresponding uncertainty spectrum derived from <math id="S4.I2.i4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐐</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>APPLICATION TO AN ASTRONOMICAL SPECTRUM</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we assess the impact of the SP approach on spectral quality of real astronomical data. We applied <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> to 36 HARPS observations of the quasar HE0515<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>4414, described in Ref. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, where they were used to put constraints on the variation of the fine-structure constant (<math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>) in a damped Lyman-<math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> system at redshift <math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\approx 1.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>1.15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\approx 1.15</annotation></semantics></math>. The observations were taken in one week of December 2018, with a total exposure time of 52h 31m. The 36 new <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> spectra were all deblazed and corrected for Earth’s motion with respect to the Solar system’s barycentre. We applied the blaze function from a DRS product, <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">HARPS_BLAZE_A.fits</span>, made from tungsten lamp observations taken on the same night as quasar spectra. Barycentric Earth radial velocity (BERV) was read from standard DRS headers and applied to the wavelength array of <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> spectra.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the spectra were combined in <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Astrocook<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">[</span><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a><span id="S5.p2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">]</span></cite></span>, using “drizzling”-like technique on a wavelength grid with a bin size of <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.830\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.830</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.830\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, matching the native pixel size of HARPS and the published DRS spectrum from Ref. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. With the drizzling approach, all contributions to each bin in the final grid are collected and weighted by their inverse variance and by the amount of superposition between the original pixel and the bin itself, achieving a statistically robust co-addition with a single rebinning procedure. In the last step, the continuum is derived by an iterative kappa-sigma clipping of absorption features and a subsequent Gaussian-kernel smoothing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 5 APPLICATION TO AN ASTRONOMICAL SPECTRUM ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> compares a small section of the HE0515<math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>4414 spectrum extracted by <span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> to the corresponding HARPS DRS spectrum, for six metal absorption transitions at the same redshift. The two extractions agree closely for most of the transitions shown (Fe <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2383" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2383</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2383</annotation></semantics></math>, Mg <span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">i</span> <math id="S5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2853" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2853</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2853</annotation></semantics></math>, Fe <span id="S5.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2587" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2587</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2587</annotation></semantics></math>, and Mg <span id="S5.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2796" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2796</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2796</annotation></semantics></math>), with no visually discernible difference in line shape. For two transitions, Fe <span id="S5.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S5.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2600" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2600</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2600</annotation></semantics></math> and Mg <span id="S5.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S5.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2804" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2804</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2804</annotation></semantics></math>, the <span id="S5.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> profile at <math id="S5.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}40\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mtext> and </mtext><mrow><mn>40</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}40\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$</annotation></semantics></math> appears visually narrower than the DRS profile near the line core. We have not yet fitted Voigt profiles for these components, so we report this as a qualitative visual impression rather than a measured effect, and we do not draw a general conclusion about resolution improvement from it. A quantitative comparison of fitted line parameters between the two extractions is left to future work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.06809v1/HE0515_velocity_plot.svg" id="S5.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/508;" width="476" height="508"></object>

Each panel shows a different transition, indicated in the top left, with the oscillator strengths in the bottom right. Two spectra are overplotted: the new spectrum produced by <span id="S5.F10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> (blue histogram) and a spectrum from the literature (red histogram), produced from the same observations using HARPS DRS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Median S/N per <math id="S5.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> bin, <span id="S5.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> vs. HARPS DRS. </table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 APPLICATION TO AN ASTRONOMICAL SPECTRUM ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the median signal-to-noise ratio per <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> velocity bin, computed in four representative wavelength windows free of all absorption, for both <span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> and the standard HARPS DRS optimal extraction. The median S/N of the <span id="S5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> extraction is consistently 1% to 5% lower than the S/N in the DRS extraction. To verify this, we calculated the numerical average of fluctuations in the unabsorbed continuum, and found it was more consistent with the DRS extraction. While initially surprising, this result can be understood as a consequence of the current modelling of the HARPS PSF. As a reminder, flux uncertainties are calculated by summing over rows of <math id="S5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐐</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is related to the calibration matrix <span id="S5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">A</span> containing PSF shapes. We know from Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> that a Gaussian PSF is insufficient to fully describe HARPS’s PSF and its asymmetry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, meaning that <span id="S5.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">A</span> is not strictly correct. Clearly, errors in <span id="S5.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">A</span> have propagated into our uncertainty estimates, leading to lower S/N. Therefore, the result obtained here is consistent with – rather than a failure of – the framework.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>RESULTS</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> is the first application of spectral perfectionism to an extremely stable high-resolution astronomical spectrograph. In this first stage, the code is written with the HARPS spectrograph in mind, but is generally applicable to any other spectrograph. The most novel aspect of this work is the use of an LFC to construct the calibration matrix <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, a crucial component for the correct functioning of the SP framework. LFC lines were used to model the spectrograph’s point-spread function, for wavelength calibration, and for order tracing. Our results can be summarised as follows:</p>
<ol id="S6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We modelled the PSF shape using a bivariate Gaussian function with seven free parameters. The machinery developed here allows mock PSFs to be created at an arbitrary position within the range covered by LFC light, i.e. in diffraction orders 89 -- 123<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                  
                  
                  
                Not including order 115, which falls in the region between the two detectors, and is, hence, inaccessible.</span></span></span> (Fig. <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.2 Simulating the PSF for an Arbitrary Position ‣ 4 HARPERFECT ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>) by interpolating between measured Gaussian profile parameters. The Gaussian cannot fully capture the asymmetries present in the PSF shape (see Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and is the immediate target for future improvement.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We mapped out PSF shape variations across the detector with unprecedented detail, sampling it every <math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 15</annotation></semantics></math> physical pixels (<math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="225\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>225</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow class="ltx_unit"><mi mathvariant="normal">µ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">225\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}</annotation></semantics></math>) along the dispersion direction. These variations are consistent with being caused by optical effects (Figs.  <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). The LFC has thus (again) proven to be a powerful tool for improving our understanding of the instrument physics. This opens the path to using the LFC for real-time instrument diagnostics and to understanding how instrument optics changes with time. In the future, the LFC could be used to study PSF variations due to thermal settling of instrument components, thermal breathing, and after interventions, among other applications.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> individually, we computed the correlation coefficient <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> between the <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> components of the PSF, which quantifies its separability directly (Fig. <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>): <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to an exactly separable PSF, while <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the degree to which the assumption underlying optimal extraction is violated. We find the HARPS PSF to be measurably non-separable across the full detector, but only weakly so, with <math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> remaining of order a few percent everywhere. This is consistent with the small but consistent S/N penalty of spectral perfectionism relative to optimal extraction reported below (item 5).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using the measured LFC line positions and their known wavelengths, we wavelength calibrated HARPS in two dimensions and traced the positions of diffraction orders with high accuracy. Our wavelength calibration matches the independent calibration performed by HARPS DRS using a ThAr lamp within <math id="S6.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>250</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Wavelength calibration residuals due to the known HARPS pixel size anomaly is approximately <math id="S6.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm$25\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>25</mn><mtext> </mtext><mrow><mi class="ltx_unit">m</mi><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">s</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm$25\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$</annotation></semantics></math> and appears every <math id="S6.I1.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\text{\,}\mathrm{pix}</annotation></semantics></math> in the dispersion direction (Fig. <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Curiously, order traces derived from LFC line centres seem to be more precise than the traces from a tungsten lamp produced by HARPS DRS, which always lays off-centre with respect to the visual geometric centre of the order (Fig. <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 The Point-spread Function, Wavelength Calibration, and Order Tracing ‣ 3 CONSTRUCTING THE CALIBRATION MATRIX ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). The reason for this is unknown and the impact on science analysis derived from DRS products is unquantified.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In a real-world application to the HARPS spectrum of the quasar HE0515<math id="S6.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>4414, the spectrum produced by <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> has a S/N that is a few percent lower than the spectrum produced by HARPS DRS (Tab. <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 APPLICATION TO AN ASTRONOMICAL SPECTRUM ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). This result should be viewed as a limitation of using a model that does not capture the true PSF shape, underlying the need to improve this aspect of the procedure to reap the full benefits of spectral perfectionism.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">6.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In a visual, unmodelled comparison of six metal absorption transitions at the same redshift (Fig. <a href="#S5.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 5 APPLICATION TO AN ASTRONOMICAL SPECTRUM ‣ “Perfect” spectra for ESO’s HARPS spectrograph" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), four show no discernible difference between <span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> and HARPS DRS, while two (Fe <span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S6.I1.i6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2600" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2600</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2600</annotation></semantics></math> and Mg <span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ii</span> <math id="S6.I1.i6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda 2804" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2804</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda 2804</annotation></semantics></math>) show apparently sharper profiles in the cores of narrow absorption components in <span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> spectra. Given the absence of quantitative Voigt profile fitting, we present this as a preliminary visual observation rather than evidence of a systematic resolution gain, particularly in light of the S/N result above.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Further improvements are expected by using a more accurate PSF model, modelling the LFC background, and compensating for the uneven pixel sizes during wavelength calibration. In its current form, <span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Harperfect</span> takes 50 seconds to processes a single box of <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096\times$60\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mn>60</mn><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi class="ltx_unit">pix</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096\times$60\text{\,}{\mathrm{pix}}^{2}$</annotation></semantics></math>, or 2 hours for the full spectrum. While this is substantially slower than optimal extraction, the increase in spectral fidelity – required for precision measurements of absorption line centroids and shapes – justifies the extra effort.</p>
</div>

</div>

</span></li>
<li id="bib.bib6" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_article"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_key ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">[6]</span>
